old_entry.title: Dragon Quest
old_entry.subtitle: Dragon Quest Teaches Console Players How to Read a Role-Playing Game
old_entry.summary: Yuji Horii, Akira Toriyama and Koichi Sugiyama helped make computer role-playing approachable on a console.
body: Enix released Dragon Quest for Famicom in Japan on May 27, 1986. Yuji Horii, Koichi Sugiyama, Akira Toriyama and the Chunsoft team condensed ideas from computer role-playing games into a form suited to controllers and console audiences. The world is small, the party initially consists of a single hero and commands are organized into readable menus. This reduction is decisive. Rather than imitating all of Western computer RPG complexity, Dragon Quest builds an accessible vocabulary that would deeply influence Japanese role-playing games.

Dragon Quest appears in a console market where many players have little experience with text commands and computer-RPG tables. Horii reduces the number of visible systems, organizes actions into menus and builds progression that is easy to understand. Simplicity is not lack of ambition but pedagogical design. Each new area gradually introduces enemies, equipment and goals. The game teaches its vocabulary while using it, creating an entry point that allows the genre to reach a much broader audience.

Moving across the map means risking random encounters that consume health and magic. Distance between towns and dungeons therefore becomes a measure of risk. New equipment does not only help win harder fights; it allows the player to travel slightly farther before returning. Progression takes the form of expanding circles around safe locations. Dragon Quest makes numerical growth understandable by translating it into geography: becoming stronger literally means being able to inhabit a larger portion of the world.

Akira Toriyama's designs give enemies a personality that survives the Famicom's limited resolution. The Slime is the clearest example: a simple shape, immediate face and almost friendly character turn the first opponent into a mascot. This readability helps combat because players quickly recognize categories and dangers, but it also builds affection. Dragon Quest demonstrates that an RPG bestiary can become part of a series' cultural identity rather than merely a ladder of increasingly high statistics.

old_entry.title: Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels
old_entry.summary: Super Mario Bros. 2, known outside of Japan as Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels, is a 1986 platform game developed by Nintendo R&D4 for the Famicom Disk System.
body: Super Mario Bros. 2, known outside of Japan as Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels, is a 1986 platform game developed by Nintendo R&D4 for the Famicom Disk System. Like its predecessor, Super Mario Bros., players control Mario or Luigi to rescue Princess Peach from Bowser. The Lost Levels has a higher difficulty level, introducing obstacles such as the Poison Mushroom, counterproductive level warps and mid-air wind gusts. Luigi controls differently from Mario, with reduced ground friction and increased jump height. The game contains 32 levels across eight worlds, and 20 bonus levels.

Nintendo developed The Lost Levels after designing some of its levels for the Nintendo VS. System version of Super Mario Bros. It was directed by Takashi Tezuka and designed for players who had mastered the original. Nintendo released it as Super Mario Bros. 2 in Japan on June 3, 1986, but Nintendo of America deemed it too difficult for the North American market and released an alternative Super Mario Bros. 2 (1988) instead. The original Super Mario Bros. 2 was retitled The Lost Levels for its inclusion in the 1993 Super Nintendo Entertainment System compilation Super Mario All-Stars, its first international release. It has been rereleased for Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, Wii, Wii U, Nintendo 3DS, and Nintendo Switch.

Reviewers viewed The Lost Levels as an extension of Super Mario Bros, especially its difficulty progression, and appreciated the challenge when spectating speedruns. The Lost Levels gave Luigi his first unique character traits, while the poison mushroom became a recurring Mario franchise element. The Lost Levels was the bestselling FDS game, selling about 2.5 million copies. It is remembered as among the most difficult Nintendo games and recognized as a precursor to the Kaizo subculture, in which fans create and share ROM hacks featuring nearly impossible levels.

On June 3, 1986 Nintendo released the direct sequel to Super Mario Bros. in Japan for the Famicom Disk System. In the West it later became known as The Lost Levels. The graphics look reassuring, but the design starts from players' accumulated skill and turns it against them: stricter jumps, poison mushrooms, wind and deceptive trajectories turn familiar rules into an advanced course in reading space.

In late 1985, during simultaneous development of The Legend of Zelda (1986), the Super Mario Bros. team began creating a version of the game for Nintendo's coin-operated arcade machine, the VS. System–while also experimenting with new, challenging level designs. They enjoyed these new levels, and thought that Super Mario devotees would too. Shigeru Miyamoto, who created the Mario franchise and directed Super Mario Bros., no longer had time to design games by himself, given his responsibilities leading Nintendo's Nintendo R&D4 division and their work on The Legend of Zelda. The Super Mario sequel was delegated to its predecessor's assistant director, Takashi Tezuka, as his directorial debut. He worked with Miyamoto and the R&D4 team to develop a sequel based on the same underlying technology, including some levels directly from Vs. Super Mario Bros. Development of the Super Mario sequel began in January 1986 and lasted about four months.

The Lost Levels is a 2D side-scrolling platform game similar in style and gameplay to the original 1985 Super Mario Bros., save for an increase in difficulty. As in the original, Mario (or Luigi) ventures to rescue the Princess from Bowser. The player jumps between platforms, avoids enemies and obstacles, finds secrets (such as backwards Warp Zones and vertical vines) and collects power-ups such as the Mushroom (which makes Mario grow), the Fire Flower (which lets Mario throw fireballs), and the Invincibility Star. Unlike the original, there is no two-player mode; however, at the title screen, the player chooses between Mario or Luigi. Their abilities are differentiated for the first time: Luigi, designed for skilled players, has slower acceleration and deceleration with a higher jump height, while Mario is the opposite; he has faster acceleration and deceleration, but has a lower jump height.

The Lost Levels continues the difficulty progression from Super Mario Bros. It introduces obstacles including Poison Mushrooms, warps that return the player to previous levels, and gusts that redirect the player midair. The Poison Mushroom, in particular, works as an anti-mushroom, shrinking or killing the player character. Some levels require "split-second" precision and others require the player to jump on invisible blocks. After each boss fight, Toad tells Mario that "[their] princess is in another castle". The main game has 32 levels across eight worlds and five bonus worlds. A hidden World 9 is accessible if the player does not use a Warp Zone. Bonus worlds A through D are accessible when the player plays through the game eight times, for a total of 52 levels.

old_entry.title: Star Soldier
old_entry.subtitle: Star Soldier Compresses Shooter Spectacle into a Test of Rhythm and Score
old_entry.summary: On June 13, 1986 Hudson Soft released Star Soldier for Famicom.
body: On June 13, 1986 Hudson Soft released Star Soldier for Famicom. The vertical shooter compresses speed, firing control and pattern memory into sessions where score becomes a form of mastery. Its importance also grows beyond the screen: in Japan it connects to the culture of Caravan timed competitions, where performance can be compared, narrated and turned into an event.

Star Soldier is a vertically scrolling shooter where the player controls the pilot and space fighter Caesar in a ship. The player can move and shoot enemies that appear from the top of the screen. Bullets from the starship can hit both flying and grounded enemies, and the player only has one shooting attack. The game has sixteen unique stages with vertically scrolling background and foreground elements.

With the scrolling background of the space station, the player may occasionally enter the "trap zone", an area where the ship can fly underneath the space station to avoid enemy fire. Shooting the "P-mark" that appears in the stages can reward the player with a capsule, a power-up that increases the power of the ship's bullets as more capsules are collected. If the capsule is not collected, the ship will move slower and only shoot one bullet at a time.

If two capsules are collected, the ship will transform and can be able to shoot from behind. If the player collects three capsules, the ship will start shooting in five directions and will summon a shield that protects the player until the ship is hit five times, with the fourth and final capsule collected being able to destroy any flying enemies. body: Ganbare Goemon! Karakuri Dōchū is a video game produced by Konami. It is the second game in the Ganbare Goemon series (sometimes known in English as Mystical Ninja) and the first to be released on a video game console and home computer. It was initially released for the Family Computer on July 30, 1986 and later released for the MSX2 a year later. The Famicom version was re-released in Japan only for the Game Boy Advance under the Famicom Mini label and for the Wii, Nintendo 3DS and Wii U under the Virtual Console service. The game is set to be re-released in 2026 via the Ganbare Goemon! Daishūgō compilation. A direct sequel, Ganbare Goemon 2, was released for the Famicom on January 4, 1989.

old_entry.summary: On August 6, 1986 Metroid debuted on the Family Computer Disk System.
body: On August 6, 1986 Metroid debuted on the Family Computer Disk System. Nintendo combined side-view action with a structure that asks players to remember doors, shafts and obstacles they cannot yet cross. Each new ability does more than make Samus stronger: it changes the player's mental map by reopening places already seen. Isolation, sound and the final reveal of the protagonist's identity complete a work that would later help give a name, alongside Castlevania, to an entire family of exploration structures.

Nintendo attempted to distinguish Metroid from other games by making it a nonlinear adventure-based game, in which exploration was a crucial part of the experience. The game often requires that the player retrace steps to progress, forcing the player to scroll the screen in all directions, as with most contemporary games. Metroid is considered one of the first video games to impress a feeling of desperation and solitude on the player. Following The Legend of Zelda, Metroid helped pioneer the idea of acquiring tools to strengthen characters and help progress through the game. Until then, most ability-enhancing power-ups like the Power Shot in Gauntlet (1985) and the Starman in Super Mario Bros. offered only temporary boosts to characters, and they were not required to complete the game. In Metroid, however, items are permanent fixtures that last until the end. In particular, missiles and the ice beam are required to finish the game.

Metroid is an action-adventure game in which the player controls Samus Aran in sprite-rendered two-dimensional landscapes. The game takes place on the planet Zebes, a large, open-ended world with areas connected by doors and elevators. The player controls Samus as she travels through the planet's caverns and hunts Space Pirates. She begins with a weak power beam as her only weapon, and with only the ability to jump. The player explores more areas and collects power-ups that grant Samus special abilities and enhance her armor and weaponry, allowing her to enter areas that were previously inaccessible. Among the power-ups that are included in the game are the Morph Ball, which allows Samus to curl into a ball to roll into tunnels; the Bomb, which can only be used while in ball form and can open hidden floor/wall paths; and the Screw Attack, a somersaulting move that destroys enemies in its path.

Tanaka said he wanted to make a score that made players feel like they were encountering a "living organism" and had no distinction between music and sound effects. The only time a melodic theme is heard is when Mother Brain is defeated in order to give the victorious player catharsis. During the rest of the game, the melodies are more minimalistic, because Tanaka wanted the soundtrack to be the opposite of the "hummable" pop tunes found in other games at that time.

old_entry.title: Starflight
old_entry.subtitle: Starflight Makes a Vast Universe Out of Limited Memory
old_entry.summary: On August 15, 1986 Starflight arrived on DOS and offered a sense of space that was startlingly large for a home computer of its era.
body: On August 15, 1986 Starflight arrived on DOS and offered a sense of space that was startlingly large for a home computer of its era. Players recruit a crew, configure a ship, explore systems, descend to planets, trade resources and follow clues about a cosmic threat. Its scale does not come from thousands of unique assets, but from systems that combine coordinates, economy and encounters. Starflight shows how the feeling of travel can depend less on the quantity of graphics than on continuity between different kinds of decisions.

Starflight has 270 star systems, each containing from zero to eight planets for a total of 800. All star systems can be entered and all planets landed on, though this destroys the ship if the gravity is greater than 8.0 g. The science officer can scan and analyze the planet for information about it, including its temperature, gravity, and chemical composition. When a landing is ordered, a Mercator projection map shows the topography of each planet, as well as a cursor to select a landing point. Once the ship lands, a Terrain Vehicle can be deployed to drive across the terrain, which is periodically scanned for new information, in search of minerals, lifeforms, and alien ruins. As is the case in outer space, a heads-up display monitors the Terrain Vehicle's status.

The player begins inside a space station called Starport orbiting the planet Arth. Here they buy and sell minerals, Endurium (fuel), and artifacts, recruit and train crew members, and upgrade parts of the ship. The player hires a crew from five species to man the ship's six posts: navigator, science officer, engineer, communications officer, doctor, and captain. A crewman's proficiency is determined by the relevant skill: a science officer with a high science skill can determine more of a planet's properties and detect aliens at a greater range, for example. Skills are increased through training, which must be purchased. One crewman can man multiple posts, but different species have different maximum skill levels. The ship is initially equipped only with engines and a limited supply of Endurium, a type of crystal used as fuel. The ship can be modified and upgraded through the purchase of weapons, armor, and shields.

Johnson was guided by his friend and office-mate Paul Reiche III, the designer of Archon, during a period where Reiche was "supposed to be working on Mail Order Monsters". Reiche advised Johnson to draft a "story network" that would highlight all the most important points of the story and list the in-game objects necessary to advance from one to the next. The designers rewrote the script multiple times. The group designed what they called a "fractal generator", which took six man-years to develop and allowed them to increase the number of planets in the game from 50 to 800. The game was one of the earliest to use procedurally-generated content for planets and everything on them. The techniques used created a type of roguelike environment on each planet, with the contents randomly distributed. The story network was also one of the earliest examples of a sandbox game design.

old_entry.title: Castlevania
old_entry.subtitle: Horror Finds a Rhythm to Learn
old_entry.summary: On September 26, 1986, Konami released Akumajō Dracula in Japan for the Famicom Disk System, the work that would originate the series known internationally as Castlevania.
body: Castlevania, known in Japan as Akumajō Dracula, is a 1986 platform game developed and published by Konami. Players control Simon Belmont, descendant of a legendary vampire hunter, who enters the castle of Count Dracula to destroy him when he suddenly reappears 100 years after Simon's ancestor vanquished him.

The whip attack has a recognizable timing and distance. Pressing the command when an enemy is already too close may not be enough because the gesture has to complete. This characteristic encourages preparation instead of always reacting at the last possible moment. Simon's body does not seek the same elasticity as other protagonists: it retains a weight that makes decisions meaningful. The player has to learn where to stop and when to commit to an action. Difficulty also grows from this temporal responsibility. A command is not merely an intention, but a choice that occupies an interval while the world continues to move. Understanding that interval allows a feeling of rigidity to be transformed into a tool of control.

The whip distinguishes Simon not only visually. It defines his relationship with enemies, offering a reach that has to be judged against their approach. The weapon therefore makes the character recognizable through a spatial relationship. There is no need to change equipment constantly in order to create variety: targets, heights and the conditions under which attacking is advantageous can change instead. This stability allows the player to refine an internal measure. They learn to feel when an opponent is within reach and when it is necessary to wait. The hero's identity thus emerges from the meeting between image and rule. The whip is a symbol because it is repeatedly used in a way that makes the entire experience distinctive, not merely because it appears in his design.

Additional weapons offer different answers, but their use depends on a resource. The player therefore has to decide when to use them and when to preserve a margin for a later encounter. The choice introduces planning into a relatively direct action path. A weapon useful in one situation may be less suitable in another, and picking up a new one requires an evaluation. The system prevents every possibility from remaining available without consequences. This economy makes certain moments easier to read: the relief of having an appropriate tool comes from knowing that it is not guaranteed. Combat concerns not only the precision of the immediate gesture, but also decisions made before reaching the obstacle, when danger was still only anticipated.

The 1986 Akumajō Dracula organizes its castle as a linear progression of rooms, stairs, platforms and encounters that ask the player to commit before fully knowing the outcome. Simon jumps along a fixed trajectory and cannot correct every mistake at the last instant, so the placement of enemies and obstacles gains precise weight. A staircase changes speed and response options; a narrow platform can turn even a common enemy into a problem of position. The level does not simply connect one boss to the next. It builds a cadence of preparation, execution and recovery. This spatial discipline makes the castle memorable from the first entry, long before the series would develop more open exploratory structures in later games.

The first Castlevania takes figures from Western horror imagery and turns them into immediately distinguishable behaviors. Bats, skeletons, armor, Medusa heads and other creatures do not merely decorate a Gothic castle: they occupy different trajectories and timings, forcing Simon to change position and priorities. Cultural recognition speeds up interpretation. Dracula, classic monsters and the architecture evoke an already familiar repertoire, but the game has to translate it into rules compatible with few colors, small sprites and two-dimensional spaces. Part of the series' identity is born in this conversion. Horror does not depend on visual realism, but on the ability to give each figure a silhouette, a rhythm and a threat that can be understood while playing.

old_entry.title: Alex Kidd in Miracle World
old_entry.subtitle: Before Sonic, SEGA Was Looking for Its Hero
old_entry.summary: On November 2, 1986, for this editorial exception in the calendar, Alex Kidd in Miracle World is associated with its Japanese debut on the Sega Mark III.
body: Alex Kidd in Miracle World is a platform game developed and published by Sega for the Master System. The player must finish levels and overcome obstacles and puzzles in both scrolling and single-screen environments. Throughout the 17 stages, Alex faces many monsters and the three henchmen of Janken the Great, before facing Janken himself.

Alex Kidd in Miracle World was born from a very concrete question: how could SEGA build a recognizable action game for the Mark III while Super Mario Bros. was consolidating the Famicom's success? In the historical interview published by SEGA, the designer recalls that the original project, called Miracle Land, was closer to an action RPG and even featured a protagonist armed with a staff. Revisions instead produced a martial-arts hero who could punch sideways and destroy parts of the scenery. Even the button layout was deliberately differentiated from Mario's, a decision the same author later judged unnatural. The historical value of these choices lies precisely in showing a team searching for its own language, experimenting with identity, controls and rhythm while the home platformer was still defining its conventions.

Miracle World avoids building the adventure around a single cadence. Alex runs and jumps, but he can also swim, cross sections on a motorcycle and pilot the Peticopter, while shops and items interrupt the purely linear flow of the platforming. This variety comes from a project that still carries traces of its more adventurous origins: the player must study blocks, decide when to spend money and adapt to vehicles with different inertia. SEGA's documentation also recalls very concrete hardware limits, such as the number of sprites available to animate certain enemies. The result is not a random collection of ideas, but a game that uses changes in rules to continually refresh the reading of space. Each vehicle alters speed, safe distance and the way obstacles must be anticipated, giving progression an almost episodic rhythm.

Boss encounters in Alex Kidd in Miracle World can culminate in a game of rock-paper-scissors, a surprising and deliberately risky choice for an action game. The SEGA interview explains that the idea arose as another attempt to differentiate the project, and that even the team debated how harsh it was to lose a life over a decision that seemed to be left to chance. In reality, the sequences were not purely random: the designer recalls that predetermined patterns were used, turning memory into a survival tool. This detour interrupts the continuity between motor skill and success, but it also makes the game immediately recognizable. Miracle World therefore captures an era in which the rules of the platformer had not yet stabilized: reflexes, purchases, vehicles and almost board-game-like rituals could coexist without having to belong to separate genres.

old_entry.title: Zanac
old_entry.subtitle: The Screen Responds to Our Habits
old_entry.summary: On November 28, 1986, Zanac arrives in Japan on the Famicom Disk System, published by Pony Canyon and developed by Compile.
body: On November 28, 1986, Zanac arrives in Japan on the Famicom Disk System, published by Pony Canyon and developed by Compile. It is not the game's first incarnation, which had already appeared on MSX, but this version deeply reworks the project and becomes one of the best known. Zanac belongs to the tradition of vertical shooters, but introduces an idea that remains interesting today: the ALC system observes player behavior and changes the intensity of enemy attacks. Firing, destroying targets and collecting power-ups do not only increase the player's strength, they can also make the system more aggressive. The result is a dynamic relationship between skill and difficulty. This is joined by an arsenal of special weapons that encourages different strategies instead of chasing a single dominant upgrade.

Zanac's most famous feature is ALC, Automatic Level of Difficulty Control. The system does not simply choose a difficulty at the start of the game: it changes enemy aggression in response to what happens during play. Some player actions can increase pressure, while destroying certain targets can reduce it. Challenge therefore becomes a variable that reacts to behavior rather than a completely predetermined curve. The solution is remarkable because it changes the meaning of common shooter actions. Accumulating power and firing continuously are not always consequence-free, and understanding the system becomes part of advanced skill. Zanac thus builds an early form of dynamic adaptation, but does so without completely hiding the relationship between cause and response.

Zanac places eight types of special weapons alongside the main fire, obtained by collecting numbered chips. Each weapon clearly changes the relationship with space: some provide protection, others pass through targets, and others cover different directions. Collecting the same number again powers up the active weapon, so the player must decide whether to invest in a familiar solution or switch tools when the situation demands it. The variety is not there merely to multiply visual effects. It creates different styles of play and encourages reading the composition of enemy attacks. In a vertical shooter where pressure can change dynamically, the arsenal becomes a way of negotiating with the system. Strategy therefore emerges from the meeting of power-ups, risk, position and the ability to anticipate what will fill the screen a few seconds later.

The November 28, 1986 date concerns the Famicom Disk System edition, not Zanac's absolute first appearance. Compile had already developed the game for MSX, and the move to Nintendo's platform involved substantial reworking of graphics, pacing and structure. This distinction prevents the game's history from being flattened into a single ideal version. In the 1980s, bringing the same project to different hardware often meant rebuilding important parts of the experience around specific memory, video, audio and control constraints. The Famicom Disk System version therefore becomes a historical object in its own right: it preserves the idea of the adaptive shooter, but presents it within a different home ecosystem and with a reach that would contribute to the later North American NES edition. To speak about Zanac is also to speak about its transformations across platforms.
